summary: Kole Jain sorts mobile swipe interactions into three groups: movement within a page, movement between pages, and swipe gestures that replace a button or reveal more context. Within a page, he takes swipeable scrolling cards from rigid to natural by opening up the easing curve for more bounce, skewing cards at the screen edge so they read as a 3D ring, and adding page indicators with a fluid, magnetic effect. Between pages, he argues transitions should follow the direction of the swipe and keep continuity, for example a card expanding to fill the screen or an image zooming in to become the next page's hero image, instead of sliding a new page in. For gestures, he recommends swipe-to-dismiss for popovers and pages, swipe-to-confirm sliders for high-impact or irreversible actions, and offering a button as well for people who don't know the gesture. For a design system, this gives a motion stance (almost never linear, the easing curve sets the tone), a set of mobile transition patterns, and the habit of pairing gestures with a visible button fallback.
key_ideas: It's the interactions that turn a UI into an experience.
Mobile swipe interactions fall into three groups: within-page navigation, between-page navigation and swipe gestures.
Because a phone is much smaller than a desktop, its screen edges can be used for unique effects, such as skewing cards off the edge or shrinking items as they approach it.
Swipeable scrolling cards beat stacking things vertically, but swiping through them feels rigid until the easing curve is opened up for more bounce, which lets them carry momentum.
A linear ease is almost never right, because things in real life speed up and slow down.
The easing curve sets the tone of the product: snappy and performant, fun and springy, or slow and smooth.
Swipeable content needs indicators, and the indicator itself can be animated with a fluid, magnetic effect.
Swipes are intuitive for people who know them, but a button should also be offered for people who don't (Gmail's swipe or tap to delete).
Page transitions feel seamless when the new background and content move in the direction of the swipe.
Continuity, such as an image zooming in to become the next page's hero image, beats sliding a new page in.
Swipe-to-dismiss is quick and often intuitive for popovers and pages; zooming the background out and moving it down when a popover opens adds to the effect.
A swipe-to-confirm slider is harder to trigger by accident than a button, so it suits high-impact or irreversible actions.
Swipe gestures can replace a button or reveal more context; once users understand they can swipe, it is generally a faster, more seamless way to use the app.

rules.rule: Avoid a linear ease for swipe and UI animations; use a curve that speeds up and slows down.
rules.why: Things in real life speed up and slow down, and easing and bounce are what make interactions feel lifelike.
rules.evidence: Almost never do you want a linear ease

rules.rule: Give swiped cards an easing curve with bounce so they carry momentum after the swipe.
rules.why: Swiping through the cards feels very rigid; opening the curve up for more bounce makes it feel much more natural.
rules.evidence: Opening up the easing curve to give it some more bounce

rules.rule: Pick the easing curve deliberately to set the product's tone: snappy and performant, fun and springy, or slow and smooth.
rules.why: Playing with the curve transforms animations and gives them tone.
rules.evidence: It also helps provide tone like snappy and performant, fun and springy, or slow and smooth

rules.rule: On mobile, prefer swipeable scrolling cards over stacking the same items vertically.
rules.why: The source says scrolling cards are better than stacking things vertically.
rules.evidence: These are better than stacking things vertically

rules.rule: Add page indicators to any swipeable set of cards.
rules.why: The source says good UX calls for adding indicators under swipeable cards.
rules.evidence: taking into account good UX, we should add some indicators

rules.rule: Pair swipe actions with a visible button (or a long-press menu) for people who don't know the gesture.
rules.why: Swipes are readily available and intuitive, but the uninitiated need another way to do the same thing.
rules.evidence: But for the uninitiated, there are also buttons to give the user options

rules.rule: Make page transitions follow the direction of the swipe, with the new background and content moving in from that direction.
rules.why: Following the swipe direction makes the motion feel natural and the transition seamless.
rules.evidence: following the direction of the swipe with a background and new content sliding up and in

rules.rule: When navigating between pages, carry an element across, such as an image that zooms in to become the new page's hero image, instead of sliding a new page in.
rules.why: It creates continuity and makes navigation much more seamless.
rules.evidence: This swipe creates continuity because we have this image actually zooming in to become the new hero image

rules.rule: Let people dismiss popovers, bottom popups and pages by swiping (swipe down for a popup from the bottom), and still include a close button.
rules.why: Swiping to dismiss is quick and often intuitive, and buttons cover the cases where it is not immediately obvious.
rules.evidence: Another great use of gestures is for dismissing popovers and pages

rules.rule: When a popover appears from the bottom, zoom the background out and move it down, and reverse that movement when the popover is dismissed.
rules.why: The source says this background movement is what really adds to the effect.
rules.evidence: the zoom out and move down of the background when the popover appears

rules.rule: Use a swipe-to-confirm slider instead of a button for high-impact or irreversible actions, such as sending an email or buying crypto.
rules.why: It is much easier to click a button by accident than to slide a slider all the way across.
rules.evidence: These are great for high impact or irreversible actions

rules.rule: Consider a swipe gesture in place of a button (such as swiping to add a friend instead of a plus button), with a fallback for people who don't know it.
rules.why: Once users understand they can swipe, it is generally a more seamless and faster way to use the app.
rules.evidence: Or we could have a swipe interaction like this to add them

rules.rule: On phones, use the screen edges for depth effects, such as skewing cards off the edge or shrinking items as they approach it, to suggest a ring or spool of content.
rules.why: A phone is much smaller than desktop, so its edges can carry unique effects that give the feeling of a spool of data under the finger.
rules.evidence: treat it as a type of horizon that shrinks things that get closer to it

rules.rule: Consider animating page indicators with a fluid, magnetic effect on swipe instead of a plain highlight.
rules.why: The source calls indicators that just highlight on swipe boring.
rules.evidence: these can be boring, just highlighting on swipe, or let's add a fluid effect on swipe that feels kind of magnetic

rules.rule: When a card opens into a full page on swipe up, expand the card and background to screen size, fade the content up and in, and finish with an elastic snap.
rules.why: The source says this makes page navigation more fluid than a plain page change.
rules.evidence: we complete the fluid look with this elastic snap at the very top

rules.rule: In step-by-step flows such as onboarding, make the next control tappable or swipeable, with motion that follows the swipe direction and wraps into the next slide.
rules.why: Making the motion follow the swipe and wrap into the next slide makes the flow super fluid.
rules.evidence: we have a button that is clickable or swipeable

decisions.question: What easing should swiped content use?

options.name: Linear ease
options.effect: Swiping through cards feels very rigid.
options.when: Almost never, according to the source.

options.name: A curve opened up with bounce
options.effect: Cards feel much more natural and carry more momentum after the swipe.
options.when: Swipeable cards and other lifelike interactions.

decisions.recommendation: Use a curve with bounce; the source says a linear ease is almost never wanted because real things speed up and slow down.
decisions.evidence: Opening up the easing curve to give it some more bounce

decisions.question: What tone should the product's motion have?

options.name: Snappy and performant
options.effect: Motion feels snappy and performant.
options.when: Not stated in the source.

options.name: Fun and springy
options.effect: Motion feels fun and springy.
options.when: Not stated in the source.

options.name: Slow and smooth
options.effect: Motion feels slow and smooth.
options.when: Not stated in the source.

decisions.evidence: It also helps provide tone like snappy and performant, fun and springy, or slow and smooth

decisions.question: How should page indicators react when someone swipes through cards?

options.name: Plain highlight
options.effect: The current dot just highlights on swipe; the source calls this boring.
options.when: Not stated in the source.

options.name: Fluid, magnetic effect
options.effect: The indicator animates with a fluid effect on swipe that feels magnetic.
options.when: When the swipe itself should feel polished; the same effect is reused for a swipe-to-add interaction.

decisions.recommendation: The source favours the fluid, magnetic indicator over the plain highlight.
decisions.evidence: Now, these can be boring, just highlighting on swipe, or let's add a fluid effect

decisions.question: How should the app move from one page to the next?

options.name: Slide a new page in
options.effect: A plain page change; the source calls it lame.
options.when: The source does not recommend it.

options.name: Swipe up to expand
options.effect: The card underneath expands to screen size, a tab expands to fill the screen, content fades up and in, and an elastic snap finishes at the top.
options.when: Opening a detail page (a recipe page in the example) from a card.

options.name: Circle wrap
options.effect: A circle expands very large and pushes the content out, circles swap, the new one shrinks back and new content moves in, wrapping into the next slide.
options.when: Step-by-step flows such as onboarding, with a button that can be tapped or swiped.

options.name: Shared image zoom
options.effect: The image zooms in to become the new page's hero image, keeping continuity.
options.when: When a simpler option is needed; the source says even this is much better than sliding a page in.

decisions.recommendation: Make transitions follow the swipe direction and keep continuity; even a simple image zoom into the hero is much better than sliding a new page in.
decisions.evidence: Navigation between pages doesn't need to be as lame as this

decisions.question: Should an action be done by a swipe gesture, a button, or both?

options.name: Button only
options.effect: Works for people who don't know the gesture, but is slower than a learned swipe (a plus button to add a friend).
options.when: Not stated as a recommendation in the source.

options.name: Swipe only
options.effect: A more seamless, faster flow once users understand they can swipe.
options.when: Not recommended alone; the source keeps a fallback.

options.name: Swipe plus a button or long-press menu
options.effect: Fast for people who know the gesture and still usable for people who don't (Gmail delete by swipe or tap).
options.when: The default the source shows across its examples.

decisions.recommendation: Both: swipes are quicker once learned, but buttons or a long-press menu should cover the uninitiated.
decisions.evidence: providing multiple ways to interact with the same UI

decisions.question: How should people confirm a high-impact or irreversible action?

options.name: Tap a button
options.effect: Much easier to trigger by accident.
options.when: Not stated in the source for risky actions.

options.name: Slide a swipe-to-confirm slider all the way across
options.effect: Takes a deliberate movement, so it is hard to trigger by accident.
options.when: High-impact or irreversible actions, such as sending an email (Resend) or purchasing crypto.

decisions.recommendation: Use the slider for high-impact or irreversible actions because it is much harder to trigger by accident.
decisions.evidence: These are great for high impact or irreversible actions such as purchasing crypto

decisions.question: How should a step-by-step flow such as onboarding move to the next slide?

options.name: A button that slides the next slide over
options.effect: A plain slide to the next step.
options.when: Not recommended in the source.

options.name: A button that can be tapped or swiped, with a circle wrap
options.effect: Motion follows the swipe direction and wraps around into the next slide, which the source calls super fluid.
options.when: Onboarding and other slide-by-slide flows.

decisions.recommendation: The source favours the tappable-or-swipeable button whose motion follows the swipe and wraps into the next slide.
decisions.evidence: instead of just a button to slide us over, we have a button that is clickable or swipeable

decisions.question: How should a popup from the bottom be dismissed?

options.name: Swipe down only
options.effect: Quick and often intuitive.
options.when: Not recommended alone; the source includes buttons too.

options.name: Swipe down plus buttons, with the background zooming out and moving down
options.effect: Clear to swipe, still usable when the gesture is not obvious, and the background movement adds to the effect.
options.when: Popups from the bottom, as in the example.

decisions.recommendation: Swipe down to dismiss, include buttons in case it is not obvious, and zoom the background out and down on open, reversing on dismiss.
decisions.evidence: buttons are included just in case it's not immediately obvious

process.detail: Decide which of the three groups the interaction belongs to: within-page navigation, between-page navigation, or a swipe gesture that replaces a button or reveals context.
Starting from swipeable scrolling cards, replace the rigid curve with one that has more bounce so the cards carry momentum.
Skew cards as they leave the screen edge, or shrink items as they approach it, so the content feels like a ring or spool under the finger.
Add page indicators under the cards, and animate them with a fluid, magnetic effect rather than a plain highlight.

process.step: Build a page change in the swipe direction
process.detail: On swipe up: expand the card underneath to screen size, expand the tab behind it to fill the screen, fade the content up and in, then finish with an elastic snap at the top.

process.step: Build a circle wrap for step flows
process.detail: Expand a circle very large while moving the content out, swap the circles, shrink the new one back down and move the new content in, following the direction of the swipe.
Keep a button (or possibly a long-press menu) for swipe actions, such as the buttons included on a swipe-dismissable popup.

caveats: Sponsor segment for Zero To Mastery (seven courses, 137 hours, over half a million Discord students, a 10% promo code); excluded from rules.
The video shows the animations on screen but states no exact values: no durations, curves, spring settings or skew angles, so 'more bounce' is qualitative.
Much of it is the creator's opinion (scrolling cards are 'better' than stacking, plain page slides are 'lame'), not tested results.
The long-press fallback is hedged in the source ('Probably'), so the fallback rule is a recommendation, not a firm requirement.
The auto-captions say 'the email sender resend'; this was read as Resend, the email sending service.
The video does not discuss reduced motion, accessibility of gestures or how swipe-only actions work with assistive tech.
The video description is cut off after 'inspired by Apple, Linear,'.
